title: Egypt's Pound Hits a Record 56 per Dollar Before Its IMF Program Ends | The Six, Ep. 11
lede: On Oct. 26, Egypt's pound passed 56 to the US dollar for the first time, three days before the central bank's first rate increase since March 2024. Since 2016 Egypt has floated or devalued its currency five times, drawn an IMF loan raised to $8 billion and signed Gulf coastal deals worth $35 billion and $29.7 billion. This episode explains how the reset worked, what the Iran war did to it, and what to watch before the IMF program ends on Dec. 15.
keyPoints: The pound hit a record low beyond 56 per dollar at the central bank on Oct. 26, 2026, against about 8.8 before the November 2016 float (LSEG; Arab Reform Initiative).

On March 6, 2024, the central bank floated the pound and raised rates 6 points to 27.25%; the pound fell from about 30.9 to near 50 and the IMF raised its loan from $3 billion to $8 billion. Abu Dhabi's ADQ had agreed a $35 billion Ras El Hekma deal weeks earlier (BNN Bloomberg; ADQ).
Remittances reached a record $47.3 billion in FY2025/26, up from $36.5 billion, and net international reserves hit a record $57.5 billion at the end of October 2026 (Central Bank of Egypt).

After the Iran war began on Feb. 28, 2026, foreign holdings of Egyptian T-bills and bonds fell about $11 billion in March, to $27.1 billion. On Oct. 29 the central bank raised its deposit rate to 20% and its lending rate to 21% (Ministry of Finance; CBE).

Urban inflation eased to 12.7% in October 2026, down from 38% in September 2023. The IMF's final review, worth about $2.3 billion, is targeted for board approval by mid-December (CAPMAS; The National).
